lead: The decision of Jerusalem goes out as a letter, carried by trusted men, and when it is read at Antioch the believers rejoice. The letter speaks a sentence the Church has made her own: “It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us”. In the Gospel Jesus gives his commandment of love, calls his disciples friends, and tells them, “You did not choose me but I chose you”. Psalm 57 gives thanks among the peoples. Today the Church also remembers St Pius V, pope.

r.h: It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us
set: The assembly chooses two leaders to go with Paul and Barnabas: Judas called Barsabbas, and Silas. Both are prophets (15:32). Silas will soon become Paul’s companion on his second journey (15:40). He is usually identified with the Silvanus named in Paul’s letters (1 Thessalonians 1:1; 2 Corinthians 1:19). The letter is addressed to Gentile believers in Antioch, Syria and Cilicia, the region where the trouble began.
str: vv. 23–29: the letter: greeting, disowning of the troublemakers, praise of Barnabas and Paul, the decision.
vv. 30–31: the letter is read at Antioch, and the believers rejoice.

¶ A note on the text: some ancient manuscripts, chiefly the so-called Western text, give the decree in a different form, without “what is strangled” and with the saying not to do to others what one would not want done to oneself.
kw: The usual word for the decision of an assembly. The Church joins the Holy Spirit to her own judgment: “to the Holy Spirit and to us”.
Only a few necessary things are asked. The apostles lay on the Gentiles no heavier burden than charity and the life of the community require.
The letter is received as paraklēsis (v. 31). The decision of the Church comes not as a weight but as comfort.
vv: though with no instructions from us,
The apostles make clear that the men who caused the trouble did not speak for them. Authority in the Church includes honestly correcting what was said in its name.
who have risked their lives for the sake of our Lord Jesus Christ.
High praise for Barnabas and Paul. The Jerusalem church stands publicly behind the missionaries.
For it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to impose on you no further burden than these essentials:
The Holy Spirit is named first. The apostles do not claim to have invented the decision; they have discerned it.
When its members read it, they rejoiced at the exhortation.
A dispute that began with dissension ends with joy. Truth spoken in charity unites.
ch: The Church has often echoed this formula, and it expresses the faith that the Holy Spirit guides the Church’s shepherds when they decide together with Peter. The episode shows how authority serves peace: the decision was reached together, sent with living witnesses, written with respect, and received with joy.

set: The farewell discourse continues. The commandment of love was first given after the washing of the feet (13:34). Here it is repeated at the beginning and end of the passage (vv. 12, 17), which frames everything in between.
str: v. 12: love one another as I have loved you.
v. 13: the greatest love: to lay down one’s life.
vv. 14–15: no longer servants but friends.
vv. 16–17: chosen and appointed to bear lasting fruit; love one another.
kw: A friend shares what he knows. The disciples are friends because the Son has made known to them all that he heard from the Father (v. 15).
The same expression as the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep (10:11).
The initiative is his. Disciples did not apply for the post; they were chosen and sent.
vv: No one has greater love than this, to lay down one’s life for one’s friends.
He speaks of his own death the next day. And Paul will add that Christ died for us while we were still sinners (Romans 5:8): he makes friends of those for whom he dies.
but I have called you friends, because I have made known to you everything that I have heard from my Father.
Friendship with God was said of Abraham (Isaiah 41:8) and Moses, who spoke with God face to face, as one speaks to a friend (Exodus 33:11). Now it is given to all disciples.
You did not choose me but I chose you.
Grace comes first. Our choice of him is always an answer to his choice of us.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the New Law is a law of love which lets us pass from the condition of a servant who does not know what his master is doing to that of a friend of Christ (CCC 1972). It also sees in v. 13 the love with which Jesus willingly offered his life (CCC 609).

rite: St Pius V (1504–1572) was a Dominican friar, Michele Ghislieri, who became pope in 1566. He put into effect the reforms of the Council of Trent, publishing the Roman Catechism, the reformed Breviary and the Roman Missal of 1570. He called Christians to pray the Rosary for the victory at Lepanto in 1571, and from this came the feast of Our Lady of the Rosary on 7 October. His optional memorial falls on 30 April. Like the apostles in today’s first reading, he served the unity of the Church by giving clear teaching for the life of the faithful.
study: Jesus calls me a friend. How would my prayer change if I spoke to him as a friend speaks to a friend?
Is there a decision of the Church that I find hard? Have I tried to read it, as the Antioch believers did, as encouragement rather than as burden?
